summary: Describes the Russian federal standard for digital signatures, GOST R 34.10-2001, for generating and verifying signatures. It is informational and not a standard of the IETF.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5832 describes how GOST R 34.10-2001 creates and verifies digital signatures using elliptic-curve operations. A verifier uses the message and public key to check whether the signature is valid.

questions: how does the gost digital signature work
how big is a gost signature
how to verify a gost r 34.10-2001 signature
subtitle: How GOST R 34.10-2001 generates and verifies elliptic-curve signatures.

tldr.problem: Developers needed an informational description of the Russian GOST R 34.10-2001 digital signature generation and verification processes.
tldr.mechanism: The signer hashes a message and combines the result with a private integer and fresh random value; verification uses the message, signature and public curve point.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5832 is Informational and not an IETF standard; the supplied metadata says RFC 7091 updates it.

today: RFC 5832 is an Informational RFC published in March 2010 and has been updated by RFC 7091. It has not been obsoleted according to the supplied metadata.

sections.title: Purpose of the Signature Scheme
sections.content:
GOST R 34.10-2001 defines procedures for generating and verifying digital signatures using points on an elliptic curve over a prime finite field. The RFC says the scheme replaced GOST R 34.10-94 to improve protection against unauthorized modification.

A signature is intended to support message integrity, evidence of authorship and protection against forgery. The scheme's security depends on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem and the hash function used.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme creates a signature that a receiver can check with a public key. The RFC says its security depends on the curve-based math and the hash function.

sections.title: Curve Parameters and Keys
sections.content:
The scheme uses a prime modulus p greater than 2^255, a curve and a subgroup with prime order q where 2^254 < q < 2^256. It also requires a base point P and a hash function that maps messages to 256-bit values.

A user's signature key is an integer d with 0 < d < q. The verification key is the curve point Q equal to d*P. The RFC does not define how key pairs or parameter sets are generated.
sections.plainLanguage: Users share agreed curve parameters. A private integer is the signing key, and multiplying the shared base point by it produces the public verification key.

sections.title: Generating a Signature
sections.content:
The signer hashes the message, converts the hash to an integer and reduces it modulo q, using 1 if the result is zero. The signer chooses a random integer k between 0 and q, computes a curve point and derives the first signature value r.

The signer calculates s from r, the private key, k and the reduced hash value. If either signature value is zero, the procedure chooses a new k; the signature is the concatenation of two 256-bit values.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer hashes the message and combines that result with the private key and a fresh random number. The output contains two 256-bit values.

sections.title: Verifying a Signature
sections.content:
The verifier splits the signature into r and s and rejects it if either is outside the range from 0 to q. The verifier hashes the received message and calculates intermediate values from the hash and signature.

The verifier combines those values with the base point and the public key to calculate a curve point. The signature is accepted if the point's x-coordinate reduced modulo q equals r; otherwise it is invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: The verifier checks that both signature values are in range, then repeats calculations using the message and public key. The signature passes only if the calculated result matches its first value.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC estimates the algorithm's current cryptographic resistance as 2^128 operations of elliptic-curve point computations on a prime modulus of order 2^256. The RFC also says the scheme relies on the security of its hash function.

The RFC's security section otherwise states that the entire document concerns security considerations. Its test parameters are recommended only for checking implementation correctness.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives an estimated resistance of 2^128 operations and says security also depends on the hash function. Its worked values are for implementation tests only.
